subsubtopic: CALL FOR REDUCTION IN INTEREST RATES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgency under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Due to the fact that the housing situation in Canada is in a horrendous state because of the high cost of land, materials, high interest rates, and a noticeable decrease in available mortgage money, forcing an increasing number of Canadians in all provinces to abandon both house building and house buying, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie):
That the government take immediate steps to reduce interest rates to a more affordable and stable level as a means of preventing further and possibly disastrous chaos in the housing market.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Recognizing that hundreds of thousands of small businesses across Canada collect sales tax on behalf of the federal government, and recognizing that this tax collection service is required by law with absolutely no compensation, and recognizing that this task adds significantly to the already heavy paperwork burden experienced by small businesses, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That this House request the Minister of Finance to provide compensation for this service by allowing small businesses to retain 3 per cent of the federal sales tax collected, up to a maximum of $1,000 annually.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, pursuant to Standing Order 43, concerning a matter of utmost importance about which I have already secured the support of the parties.
Considering that the Third Conference on the Law of the Sea opened in 1974 at the United Nations; considering the decision reached at the end of the Ninth Session of the Conference to conclude the negotiations during the Tenth Session, so that a new Law of the Sea Charter may be adopted and signed here at the end of 1981; considering also the limited progress made during the first part of the Tenth Session which ended last weekend in New York City, due in part to the desire of the United States of America to carry out a complete revision of the results achieved to date at the Conference before adopting its final recommendations, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond-South-Delta (Mr. Siddon):
That this House reaffirm the support given by the Canadian people to the basic objectives of the Third Conference of the Law of the Sea and urge the United States Administration to undertake forthwith the revision of the draft Convention in order to increase the chances of concluding the work of the Conference when the Tenth Session resumes in Geneva in August 1981.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT PLANS TO DEAL WITH INFLATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and it touches on the sad record we are experiencing in this country with respect to inflation. I wonder if the Prime Minister would indicate if he has noticed that inflation in the United States has come down quite dramatically in the last quarter, having reached a 7.8 per cent level, while the inflation level in Canada is well over 12 per cent. If he indicates to the House that he has noticed this, would he also indicate if he plans any new measures to try to curb inflation in this country, or are we to assume that the government is content to continue to fiddle while our economy is literally being burned by inflation?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT PLANS TO DEAL WITH INFLATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it has often been said that inflation affects everybody, but it is affected by everybody as well. In his budget the Minister of Finance has clearly indicated that the fight against inflation was a priority for this government. The hon. member gives the statistics for the first quarter of this year concerning a decline in inflation in the United States. If corresponding figures for the first quarter were available in Canada, we could make a comparison. The figures quoted by the hon. member to draw a parallel with Canada are not those of the same quarter since they apply to another quarter. Therefore, we cannot make a comparison between different quarters.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EFFECT OF INFLATION ON FARMERS AND SMALL BUSINESSMEN
EFFECT OF INFLATION ON FARMERS AND SMALL BUSINESSMEN
speechtext:
If the Prime Minister chooses to duck out on answering to the House with respect to inflation, perhaps I could put a further question to the Minister of State for Finance who, I think, gave a pathetic answer to my original question. Of course we all know that inflation affects everyone. Would the minister indicate if he is aware that it affects the farmer to the extent that almost 100 per cent more farmers went bankrupt last year than the year before as a result of rising interest rates and inflationary pressures?
Second, small businessmen, in higher and higher numbers, are going under in this country as the result of the government's stubbornness in not digging in and doing something about inflation and lowering inflation rates.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subtopic: EFFECT OF INFLATION ON FARMERS AND SMALL BUSINESSMEN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say that the hon. member is particularly set upon the phenomenon of interest rates. He ought to know himself that, according to the method used in Canada,
those interest rates do reflect inflationary expectations and that until such times as all economic agents are truly determined to launch a genuine and effective fight against inflation those pressures on interest rates will remain. Madam Speaker, the hon. member refers as well to the category of agricultural producers. I am convinced that if he were to examine the output of agricultural producers and the situation, he would realize that the situation is excellent and that the programs designed especially for agricultural producers and implemented by the Minister of Agriculture protect them against rising interest rates. I would also like to add that any individual, any class in society, be they agricultural producers, small businessmen or private individuals, must share the costs that a society must bear, namely, the cost of inflation.

subtopic: EFFECT OF INFLATION ON FARMERS AND SMALL BUSINESSMEN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my last supplementary question is for the same minister who says that interest rates are governed by the expectation of inflation. Does the minister not realize it is his government that is triggering the inflation?

subtopic: EFFECT OF INFLATION ON FARMERS AND SMALL BUSINESSMEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EFFECT OF INFLATION ON FARMERS AND SMALL BUSINESSMEN
speechtext: If the minister does realize that, would he indicate to the House whether he is content to see interest rates in this country stay at the peak level of something over 18 per cent as far as the prime lending rate is concerned, while the American rate has fallen 4 per cent compared to the U.S. peak level? Could the minister explain that to the House?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subtopic: EFFECT OF INFLATION ON FARMERS AND SMALL BUSINESSMEN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I appreciate that the hon. member was not on the government side long enough to know that the action any government can take is limited. He is still nursing certain illusions which he has been entertaining for a number of years and which, fortunately or unfortunately for the economy of our country, he will continue to have for a few years yet. I should also like to indicate to him that if he draws a comparison between current interest rates on certain shortterm commercial instruments in the United States and in Canada, he will find out that the gap between the interest rates on those instruments is getting ever narrower, so that Canadian interest rates are not overvalued but they do reflect market trends and the over-all economic situation.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is obvious the Prime Minister does not see fit to address questions about inflation. He is above all those matters of importance to average Canadians.

The Prime Minister wrestled inflation to the ground.

In view of doubts expressed by two national organizations about the accuracy of the Consumer Price Index, and since even according to Statistics Canada we are now one tenth of a percentage point away from the highest rate of inflation in modern times, can the minister of many hats-and I hope he is wearing his hat as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs today-say what steps he will take to protect the consumer from the ever-increasing pressure of inflation? speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Sometime ago I was ready to rule on points of order which were raised by the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville (Mr. Cossitt) and the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), but they were absent from the House. I see that they are both present today. Their points of order concerned the use of the words "obstruct" and "obstruction", which were said to be unparliamentary. I gave a preliminary ruling at the time these matters were raised, but I also said that I would like to look into the matter further. I do not want to go into all of the meanings which one can ascribe to the words "obstruction" or "obstructionist", but I will quote from a ruling given by my predecessor, Mr. Speaker Jerome, on May 26, 1975, wherein he said:
In respect of the word "obstruction", several meanings have been ascribed to it. One does not have to examine the precedents. It is not an infrequent occurrence in this House that one side refers to the actions of the other side as being an obstruction of one kind or another, so much so that on one occasion where precedent does provide some assistance the use of the word "obstruction" in respect of an individual and specific member was found to be not out of order...
At that time it was the hon. member for York-Peel who was allowed to use the word "obstruction" in reference to another member. The usage at that time was not judged to be unparliamentary; therefore I would be hard pressed to determine now that the word is unparliamentary.

speechtext:
The House resumed debate on the motion of Mr. Chretien, seconded by Mr. Roberts, for an Address to Her Majesty the Queen respecting the Constitution of Canada.
And on the amendment of Mr. Epp, seconded by Mr. Baker (Nepean-Carleton)-That the motion be amended in Schedule B of the proposed resolution by deleting Clause 46, and by making all necessary changes to the Schedule consequential thereto.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to finish the remarks I started some time ago on this resolution. I am mindful of the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Vancouver that if the country splits up over his constitutional resolution then the country is not worth saving. What an arrogant, narrow attitude for a Prime Minister to have.
Before I leave the first schedule and move on to the charter of rights, I would like to refer to the part of the resolution which would repeal Section 20 of the British North America Act. Section 20 reads as follows:
There shall be a Session of the Parliament of Canada once at least in every Year, so that Twelve Months shall not intervene between the last Sitting of the Parliament in one Session and its first Sitting in the next Session.
I must ask what the Prime Minister's purpose is in seeking to have Section 20 repealed. Why should we give any Prime Minister, especially the present one, the right to call Parliament into session or not call it into session, as he wishes? Should the Prime Minister be allowed to run the country without having to convene Parliament? In theory and in practice, if Section 20 is repealed, a Prime Minister could run the country for a year, or even longer, as his private fiefdom, substituting orders in council for acts of Parliament.
In the second place, I cannot think of one single reason why anyone would want to wipe this or any other item of Canadian history off the books. To do so would not serve any useful purpose or add anything to the sense or purpose of this document. What it does is point to the sinister purpose behind the inclusion of this schedule in the resolution and, indeed, the whole resolution itself.

April 21, 1981

The Constitution
For the benefit of those members who still feel that they can vote for this resolution, I would like to read Section 58(2) of Part VIII of this resolution. Those members who tell their constituents that they are voting for this bill so that we can bring home the British North America Act and amend it here in Canada will have a lot to answer for if this resolution is approved by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and imposed on our country. Section 58(2) reads:
The Constitution of Canada includes,
(a)	the Canada Act,
(b)	the Acts and orders referred to in Schedule I; and
(c)	any amendment to any Act or order referred to in paragraph (a) or (b).
There can be no doubt as to the meaning of Section 58. What we are debating here is the new Constitution of Canada, to replace the BNA Act of 1867 and all its subsequent amendments. Paragraph (c) clearly states that when the Parliament of Canada makes any amendments to our Constitution, assuming this bill becomes law, such amendments will be to the Prime Minister's Constitution and not to the one we have lived under for the past 114 years.
I would like to voice my objections to some of the specific items in the resolution, in the unhappy event that it should become the new Constitution of Canada. Commencing with the preamble, I would like to address myself to the motion put forward on behalf of my party by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). I cannot understand how anyone could object to this motion. It is basic and fundamental to the founding principles of our nation. Our motion reads:
Affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free individuals and free institutions.
In his statement before the joint Senate-House of Commons committee on the Constitution, the hon. member for Provencher went on to say:
-affirming also that individuals and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law.
I have on my desk some of the representations made to me on this subject by my constituents in Victoria-Haliburton. These are in response to a newspaper release that I sent out, in which I noted that the unholy alliance of the Liberals and NDP in this House rejected our motion. I might add that I have to date received not one piece of correspondence supporting the Liberal-NDP position, but I have received well over two thousand responses supporting the position of my party.
I have been a little surprised, but very pleased, that all of the mail I have received in response to the position I have taken on the issues of the supremacy of God, abortion, the right to own and hold property and capital punishment has supported my stand all the way. I feel that I am representing the views and convictions of the majority of my people.
On the question of abortion, I reject out of hand any motion that the expectant mother should be the sole arbiter as to whether she will or will not abort a foetus. That would be tantamount to giving pregnant women decision-making powers
that are rightly those of the courts and the medical profession. I am deeply disturbed as it is by reports that some courts have ruled that a foetus does not have the status of a person until it is delivered. I suggest that that is why some people want to specify in our charter of rights that only persons have rights.
It is an established fact that a foetus is a living thing, medically, morally and spiritually, and yet, if we are to accept recent court rulings on the subject, the foetus does not have any rights until it has been delivered. This raises the very serious question as to who is to speak for the foetus until it is delivered. It is we who must answer the question. It is our responsibility, and we must decide how best to protect the foetus until it is delivered and becomes a person under the law.
Abortion must not be allowed to become a political football. It is one of the most serious social and moral issues facing our society. But it is more than just that; it is a matter of life or death. I totally reject the concept of abortion on demand. To me, it is unthinkable. We must not accept abortion as just another method of birth control. Basic standards of moral conduct rule out abortion as a means of escaping the consequences of permissive and irresponsible lifestyles.
To return to the statement on Conservative Party policy, presented to the constitutional committee by my friend, the hon. member for Provencher, I draw the attention of the House to page 6 of his statement, wherein he states our policy with regard to right of ownership of property. This statement seeks to amend Section 7 of the resolution by substituting the following:
Everyone has the right of life, liberty, security of the person and the enjoyment of property and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with principles of natural justice.
I find it difficult to understand how anyone could quarrel with this statement of principle, especially in a country where the right to own and hold property has been a fundamental right since confederation.
Here again the Liberals and NDP joined forces to oppose this motion, but I was surprised and pleased some time ago to hear that the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) spoke out in support of this motion in his remarks in this House on the Constitution resolution. On page 8135 of Hansard for Wednesday, March 11, the member for Winnipeg North quoted from the fifth amendment to the American constitution. I quote the member as follows:
-no person shall be "deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law".
The member for Winnipeg North might have completed the amendment by adding: "nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation".
The point is that the member stated that this provision is in the resolution that we are debating, and that he supports it. I am pleased to have his support for the principle of our motion, but unfortunately the right to own property is not contained in the government's version of the resolution. However, I would like to take the member's words in Hansard literally and to hope that he will stand by his guns and insist that this provision be included in Section 7 of the resolution, as it now
